sentences.text: Enoch is a machine-learning date-prediction model for the Dead Sea Scrolls, trained on radiocarbon-dated samples, together with the study that introduces it, in the Revelation First record's kind, which names it 'Enoch: dating ancient manuscripts with radiocarbon and AI-based writing-style analysis'; the study presents it as 'an AI-based date-prediction model, trained on the basis of 24 14 C-dated scroll samples' (PLOS One, 2025, and its NIH copy).

The Jerusalem Post and the European Research Council describe the Groningen researchers' combination of radiocarbon dating with handwriting analysis to date individual scrolls, and Wikipedia, which has no article on the model, gives it in its articles on the Dead Sea Scrolls and on their carbon dating as an AI-based 'date-prediction model called "Enoch"', trained on 24 radiocarbon-dated samples, for the dating of some 135 undated manuscripts.

The study is by Popović, Dhali, Schomaker, van der Plicht, Lund Rasmussen, La Nasa and colleagues, published in PLOS One on 4 June 2025 and funded by the European Research Council under grant 640497 (HandsandBible), the project the ERC names The Hands that Wrote the Bible, its lead author at the Qumran Institute of the University of Groningen (PLOS One; NIH copy; ERC); the record gives the operator as Popović and colleagues at Groningen and partners, ERC-funded, and the entity's address as the article's DOI.

The article is open access under the Creative Commons Attribution License, with its data, code and test film on Zenodo (PLOS One); the record gives data access as an open-access article and the licence as 'the article's copyright line names Popović et al. (licence text not read)', leaves the model's code and data and the scimex release unchecked, and dates the study as historical, published 2025-06-04, read 2026-10-30.

The problem it answers is stated in the study's first sentence, that dating the scrolls by palaeography is essential 'but there is an almost complete lack of date-bearing manuscripts', the record carrying that sentence as a stated limit; palaeography dates manuscripts by their handwriting, and its subjectivity and unmeasurable features 'poses a problem' (PLOS One, whose references for the method include studies of early Christian codices and early New Testament manuscripts), it 'lacks a solid empirical foundation due to the absence of securely dated reference materials' (ERC), and radiocarbon dating 'is a destructive method' (Popović, in the Jerusalem Post).

The archive's Revelation First thesis holds of the same kind of evidence, on the New Testament, that 'Papyrological dates are ranges, not certainties', and that where composition dates are inferential and manuscript dates contestable ranges, 'material attestation must be allowed to unsettle inherited priority' (#202, claim 3); its mint names this papyrological sovereignty: 'The authority of the material manuscript record over inferential chronology' (#860, RF-M01).

The papyrological inversion that thesis rests on, the earliest physical New Testament witness Johannine (𝔓52, commonly dated c. 125 CE) and the earliest copy of the Apocalypse (𝔓98) older than the earliest copy of Romans (𝔓46) (#202), takes its first receipt from a handwriting date: 'Gospel of John (𝔓52): c. 125 CE (Hadrianic handwriting baseline)' (#832).

The model's anchors are radiocarbon: the team dated 30 manuscripts from four sites spanning about five centuries, 27 dates were valid, and 24 form its primary training set (PLOS One), 'two dozen scrolls, from four different sites in the Judean Desert' in BAS's account; one of the radiocarbon results, 4Q114, a fragment of Daniel 8–11, falls at 230–160 BCE, overlapping the period in which the end of Daniel was presumably written (PLOS One).

It applies Bayesian ridge regression to angular and allographic writing-style features of the ink traces, depending on no pre-trained model and trained on no palaeographic estimates, and in the study 'style' 'is not related to textual content or wording' (PLOS One); its features 'have a solid basis in writer identification', and BAS writes that 'In effect, the model performs its own comparative paleographic analysis', while the record's method and unit restate the study: regression on writing-style feature vectors, trained on 24 radiocarbon-dated samples and applied to 135 undated scrolls, each date predicted 'from the angular and allographic features of its handwriting'.

The archive reads that basis at its own grain: writer identification establishes that 'Handwriting is individuating at a statistically demonstrable level' given sufficient sample and cannot 'Attribute a single short inscription with forensic confidence', its accuracy degrading 'sharply on short samples' (#1443, §5.1), and the archive's specification of the machine-eligible handwritten artifact takes the computational validation of handwriting, its 'discriminating elements are measurable and individuating', into its own genealogy (#1409, §I.2).

Against the radiocarbon dates the model's mean absolute error is 27.9 to 30.7 years (PLOS One; the record's first finding); applied to 135 undated scrolls, its predictions were 'aligning with 79% in palaeographic post-hoc evaluation', 107 realistic and 28 not, with a 7% margin (PLOS One; NIH copy), an evaluation made by 'Expert palaeographers among the article’s authors' (PLOS One); the record carries the 79% alignment as a stated limit, beside its count, 24 samples and 135 scrolls as of 4 June 2025, and its coverage, the Judaean Desert in the Hellenistic and Roman periods.

The study answers the objection that the predictions echo their radiocarbon training with leave-one-out validation and holds that '14 C date ranges are evidently superior to style-based predictions' (PLOS One), where the ERC says the model predicts within about 30 years, 'more accurate than standalone radiocarbon dating in this period'; the Jerusalem Post gives the 135 scrolls as spanning about 200 BCE to 100 CE.

The finding, in the study's words, is that the radiocarbon ranges and the model's predictions 'are often older than traditionally assumed palaeographic estimates, leading to a new chronology of the scrolls', the Herodian script emerging earlier than thought, beside the Hasmonaean (PLOS One; the record's second finding; Wikipedia: 'earlier dates and coexistence of the Herodian and Hasmonean scripts').

Two different results carry the headline: the radiocarbon date of 4Q114 and the model's third-century BCE prediction for 4Q109, a copy of Ecclesiastes, which together, the study says, 'establish these to be the first known fragments of a biblical book from the time of their presumed authors' (PLOS One); the Jerusalem Post and the ERC report the pair, Wikipedia gives 4Q114 as 'as much as 60 years earlier than previously thought', and Christopher Rollston, in BAS, calls the 4Q114 range 'Enoch’s calibrated date range' and judges it too high, since Daniel 7–12 cannot be dated before 167 BCE.

What the model dates is the copy: the record's negative tag is 'NOT a composition date: it dates the copies', and among what the evidence does not answer is 'when any work copied on a scroll was composed' (Revelation First record); the study's own claims are stated of copies, fragments from the time of their 'presumed authors' and literary manuscripts copied before the Hasmonaean expansion (PLOS One; Jerusalem Post), and BAS reports texts associated with the Qumran community dated before the site's first settlement.

The archive states the distinction as a rule of its own dating argument: 'Manuscript attestation does not equal composition date' (#832, with its later versions and the Josephus-thesis papers), its papyrological section 'does not argue that papyrological dating of copies establishes composition dates' (#832), and its mint autograph inference holds that 'All NT dating is autograph inference — the autograph is lost; what survives is copies of copies' (#860, RF-M19).

The record keeps the study's object apart from the New Testament, 'NOT a New Testament study: Hebrew and Aramaic scrolls', with 'the dates of Greek New Testament papyri (not in its corpus)' among what it does not answer, and gives what it answers as 'how far palaeographic dates of the scrolls move against radiocarbon anchors' and that a style-based model can date undated manuscripts 'within about thirty years on this corpus' (Revelation First record).

The record files it under three of the census's four intersections, AI and ancient texts, papyrology and discovery, and New Testament scholarship, with machine, radiocarbon and palaeographic dating as its kinds of evidence, the Dead Sea Scrolls as its text object and the scrolls' digital library as the corpus it uses, in a census whose question is 'What evidence does each resource hold on when and from what the New Testament writings were composed, and how do machines now read those texts?' and whose correction is 'Revelation First ≠ Revelation Early' (Revelation First record).

On the record's reading the bearing is on dating: 'New Testament papyri are dated by palaeography alone, and this study moves palaeographic dates earlier against radiocarbon anchors'; it 'does not date New Testament papyri' and is 'the method the papyrological-inversion and dating workstreams would watch' (Revelation First record, rf_intersection), and the thesis those workstreams serve states its first falsifier as a matter of secure dating, 'a document in the NT can be securely dated earlier than any plausible date for Revelation' (#202).

The census's worked questions give the ground: 'A papyrus dates its copy, and the composition must come before it', and most early New Testament papyri are dated by handwriting alone, where Enoch stands as 'a method that moves palaeographic dates earlier against radiocarbon anchors, on the Dead Sea Scrolls'; machine dating 'is calibrated on a corpus', Enoch's style-based dates are 'often older than palaeographic estimates', and none of the four machine-reading resources 'dates a New Testament papyrus or a composition' (Revelation First, questions papyri-revelation-date and machine-dating).

The study offers its dates as 'probability-based options' to aid palaeographers and historians, claims to be 'the first complete machine-learning-based model' of its kind with an 'explainable design', calls itself 'a first step' whose advantage is 'quantified objectivity to palaeography' (also in the Jerusalem Post), and leaves 'black box' pre-trained models as a future option that depends on palaeographers' acceptance (PLOS One); its authors say it opens the ancient world 'like a time machine' (Jerusalem Post, after Ars Technica), and the ERC calls it 'a robust and objective framework for dating over a thousand manuscripts'.

The archive's survey of machine reading reads the same design at Ithaca: the hazard of a machine's early reading 'is a property of single-verdict interfaces, not of machine reading as such', ranked alternatives are its mitigation, and Ithaca's gain comes from interface design, ranked hypotheses that the historian evaluates 'rather than accepting an answer' (#1443, §2.3); such systems 'work on authors who cannot be consulted' (#1443).

The study sets itself beside Ithaca, which combined AI and epigraphy to date Greek inscriptions (PLOS One), and Haaretz's card opens 'From Ithaca to Judea Enoch is not the first artificial intelligence used to study ancient texts'; after it, Popović plans to apply the model to more scrolls and to Aramaic texts such as the Elephantine Papyri (Jerusalem Post), and Wikipedia records a five-year project he leads with the Israel Antiquities Authority, announced in June 2026, a distinct project.

The study's limits stand with its findings: for 11Q5 it gives a date after 100 CE, against the reconstruction that the scrolls were hidden before summer 68 CE; its results are 'the first published results on date estimation for this collection', with validation to come, though it dates both halves of the Great Isaiah Scroll to one period; and its Herodian-type dates challenge the default typology, where 'More research is needed to solve this issue' (PLOS One).

Reception divides, 'not all scholars are convinced' (BAS): Rollston finds the results 'not earth-shattering' and mostly what Frank Moore Cross had stated sixty years earlier, Ben-Dov finds points 'we would have otherwise missed' and asks whether the study is 'reliable enough to substantiate a re-shuffle of the entire chronological paradigm of Qumran', and Adler calls it 'a way to move forward' (BAS).

The press gives the shift a size the study does not, which says 'often older': the Jerusalem Post, 'by 50 to 150 years earlier than previously believed', Popović, 'dates that are 50 years older or maybe even a century older', and a Reddit card, 'up to 100 years older'; video cards title it 'How AI Redated the Dead Sea Scrolls' and 'AI Just Decoded the Dead Sea Scrolls — What It Found Changes Everything', and a National Geographic UK post's title is cut at 'By combining time honoured excavation techniques'.

At the name 'Enoch AI dating Dead Sea Scrolls' on Google's AI Overview, signed out, on 2026-10-31, a new address whose record was built the day before and which no card cites, the composition holds the study's figures, the 24 samples, the method, the roughly thirty-year error and 79% of 135, and keeps copies apart from their authors, 'the distinction the field turns on' (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31).

The registry records its departures, 'a significant portion … 50 to 150 years older' for the study's 'often older', the radiocarbon date of 4Q114 credited to the model, figures for 4Q109 not in the saved sources, the study's own limit unsaid while doubt goes to Reddit and Popović's caution to Haaretz, and the study's frame surviving only as what 'Supporters view'; its reader noted the first two departures without charging them and found the funder and the commitments absent, and its analysis is that the study is 'composed nearly at its own grain', its 'figures grow where the press rounded them, and its doubts are sourced to a forum' (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31).

The name is shared: the study says the model is 'named after the ancient Jewish science hero', and Wikipedia's disambiguation page gives the bare name as a biblical figure, the subject of the Book of Enoch, and lists no model (Wikipedia, Enoch (disambiguation)).

L_BA.text: Enoch is a machine-learning date-prediction model for the Dead Sea Scrolls, trained on radiocarbon-dated samples, together with the study that introduces it, in the Revelation First record's kind, which names it 'Enoch: dating ancient manuscripts with radiocarbon and AI-based writing-style analysis'; the study presents it as 'an AI-based date-prediction model, trained on the basis of 24 14 C-dated scroll samples' (PLOS One, 2025, and its NIH copy). The Jerusalem Post and the European Research Council describe the Groningen researchers' combination of radiocarbon dating with handwriting analysis to date individual scrolls, and Wikipedia, which has no article on the model, gives it in its articles on the Dead Sea Scrolls and on their carbon dating as an AI-based 'date-prediction model called "Enoch"', trained on 24 radiocarbon-dated samples, for the dating of some 135 undated manuscripts. The study is by Popović, Dhali, Schomaker, van der Plicht, Lund Rasmussen, La Nasa and colleagues, published in PLOS One on 4 June 2025 and funded by the European Research Council under grant 640497 (HandsandBible), the project the ERC names The Hands that Wrote the Bible, its lead author at the Qumran Institute of the University of Groningen (PLOS One; NIH copy; ERC); the record gives the operator as Popović and colleagues at Groningen and partners, ERC-funded, and the entity's address as the article's DOI. The article is open access under the Creative Commons Attribution License, with its data, code and test film on Zenodo (PLOS One); the record gives data access as an open-access article and the licence as 'the article's copyright line names Popović et al. (licence text not read)', leaves the model's code and data and the scimex release unchecked, and dates the study as historical, published 2025-06-04, read 2026-10-30. The problem it answers is stated in the study's first sentence, that dating the scrolls by palaeography is essential 'but there is an almost complete lack of date-bearing manuscripts', the record carrying that sentence as a stated limit; palaeography dates manuscripts by their handwriting, and its subjectivity and unmeasurable features 'poses a problem' (PLOS One, whose references for the method include studies of early Christian codices and early New Testament manuscripts), it 'lacks a solid empirical foundation due to the absence of securely dated reference materials' (ERC), and radiocarbon dating 'is a destructive method' (Popović, in the Jerusalem Post). The archive's Revelation First thesis holds of the same kind of evidence, on the New Testament, that 'Papyrological dates are ranges, not certainties', and that where composition dates are inferential and manuscript dates contestable ranges, 'material attestation must be allowed to unsettle inherited priority' (#202, claim 3); its mint names this papyrological sovereignty: 'The authority of the material manuscript record over inferential chronology' (#860, RF-M01). The papyrological inversion that thesis rests on, the earliest physical New Testament witness Johannine (𝔓52, commonly dated c. 125 CE) and the earliest copy of the Apocalypse (𝔓98) older than the earliest copy of Romans (𝔓46) (#202), takes its first receipt from a handwriting date: 'Gospel of John (𝔓52): c. 125 CE (Hadrianic handwriting baseline)' (#832). The model's anchors are radiocarbon: the team dated 30 manuscripts from four sites spanning about five centuries, 27 dates were valid, and 24 form its primary training set (PLOS One), 'two dozen scrolls, from four different sites in the Judean Desert' in BAS's account; one of the radiocarbon results, 4Q114, a fragment of Daniel 8–11, falls at 230–160 BCE, overlapping the period in which the end of Daniel was presumably written (PLOS One). It applies Bayesian ridge regression to angular and allographic writing-style features of the ink traces, depending on no pre-trained model and trained on no palaeographic estimates, and in the study 'style' 'is not related to textual content or wording' (PLOS One); its features 'have a solid basis in writer identification', and BAS writes that 'In effect, the model performs its own comparative paleographic analysis', while the record's method and unit restate the study: regression on writing-style feature vectors, trained on 24 radiocarbon-dated samples and applied to 135 undated scrolls, each date predicted 'from the angular and allographic features of its handwriting'. The archive reads that basis at its own grain: writer identification establishes that 'Handwriting is individuating at a statistically demonstrable level' given sufficient sample and cannot 'Attribute a single short inscription with forensic confidence', its accuracy degrading 'sharply on short samples' (#1443, §5.1), and the archive's specification of the machine-eligible handwritten artifact takes the computational validation of handwriting, its 'discriminating elements are measurable and individuating', into its own genealogy (#1409, §I.2). Against the radiocarbon dates the model's mean absolute error is 27.9 to 30.7 years (PLOS One; the record's first finding); applied to 135 undated scrolls, its predictions were 'aligning with 79% in palaeographic post-hoc evaluation', 107 realistic and 28 not, with a 7% margin (PLOS One; NIH copy), an evaluation made by 'Expert palaeographers among the article’s authors' (PLOS One); the record carries the 79% alignment as a stated limit, beside its count, 24 samples and 135 scrolls as of 4 June 2025, and its coverage, the Judaean Desert in the Hellenistic and Roman periods. The study answers the objection that the predictions echo their radiocarbon training with leave-one-out validation and holds that '14 C date ranges are evidently superior to style-based predictions' (PLOS One), where the ERC says the model predicts within about 30 years, 'more accurate than standalone radiocarbon dating in this period'; the Jerusalem Post gives the 135 scrolls as spanning about 200 BCE to 100 CE. The finding, in the study's words, is that the radiocarbon ranges and the model's predictions 'are often older than traditionally assumed palaeographic estimates, leading to a new chronology of the scrolls', the Herodian script emerging earlier than thought, beside the Hasmonaean (PLOS One; the record's second finding; Wikipedia: 'earlier dates and coexistence of the Herodian and Hasmonean scripts'). Two different results carry the headline: the radiocarbon date of 4Q114 and the model's third-century BCE prediction for 4Q109, a copy of Ecclesiastes, which together, the study says, 'establish these to be the first known fragments of a biblical book from the time of their presumed authors' (PLOS One); the Jerusalem Post and the ERC report the pair, Wikipedia gives 4Q114 as 'as much as 60 years earlier than previously thought', and Christopher Rollston, in BAS, calls the 4Q114 range 'Enoch’s calibrated date range' and judges it too high, since Daniel 7–12 cannot be dated before 167 BCE. What the model dates is the copy: the record's negative tag is 'NOT a composition date: it dates the copies', and among what the evidence does not answer is 'when any work copied on a scroll was composed' (Revelation First record); the study's own claims are stated of copies, fragments from the time of their 'presumed authors' and literary manuscripts copied before the Hasmonaean expansion (PLOS One; Jerusalem Post), and BAS reports texts associated with the Qumran community dated before the site's first settlement. The archive states the distinction as a rule of its own dating argument: 'Manuscript attestation does not equal composition date' (#832, with its later versions and the Josephus-thesis papers), its papyrological section 'does not argue that papyrological dating of copies establishes composition dates' (#832), and its mint autograph inference holds that 'All NT dating is autograph inference — the autograph is lost; what survives is copies of copies' (#860, RF-M19). The record keeps the study's object apart from the New Testament, 'NOT a New Testament study: Hebrew and Aramaic scrolls', with 'the dates of Greek New Testament papyri (not in its corpus)' among what it does not answer, and gives what it answers as 'how far palaeographic dates of the scrolls move against radiocarbon anchors' and that a style-based model can date undated manuscripts 'within about thirty years on this corpus' (Revelation First record). The record files it under three of the census's four intersections, AI and ancient texts, papyrology and discovery, and New Testament scholarship, with machine, radiocarbon and palaeographic dating as its kinds of evidence, the Dead Sea Scrolls as its text object and the scrolls' digital library as the corpus it uses, in a census whose question is 'What evidence does each resource hold on when and from what the New Testament writings were composed, and how do machines now read those texts?' and whose correction is 'Revelation First ≠ Revelation Early' (Revelation First record). On the record's reading the bearing is on dating: 'New Testament papyri are dated by palaeography alone, and this study moves palaeographic dates earlier against radiocarbon anchors'; it 'does not date New Testament papyri' and is 'the method the papyrological-inversion and dating workstreams would watch' (Revelation First record, rf_intersection), and the thesis those workstreams serve states its first falsifier as a matter of secure dating, 'a document in the NT can be securely dated earlier than any plausible date for Revelation' (#202). The census's worked questions give the ground: 'A papyrus dates its copy, and the composition must come before it', and most early New Testament papyri are dated by handwriting alone, where Enoch stands as 'a method that moves palaeographic dates earlier against radiocarbon anchors, on the Dead Sea Scrolls'; machine dating 'is calibrated on a corpus', Enoch's style-based dates are 'often older than palaeographic estimates', and none of the four machine-reading resources 'dates a New Testament papyrus or a composition' (Revelation First, questions papyri-revelation-date and machine-dating). The study offers its dates as 'probability-based options' to aid palaeographers and historians, claims to be 'the first complete machine-learning-based model' of its kind with an 'explainable design', calls itself 'a first step' whose advantage is 'quantified objectivity to palaeography' (also in the Jerusalem Post), and leaves 'black box' pre-trained models as a future option that depends on palaeographers' acceptance (PLOS One); its authors say it opens the ancient world 'like a time machine' (Jerusalem Post, after Ars Technica), and the ERC calls it 'a robust and objective framework for dating over a thousand manuscripts'. The archive's survey of machine reading reads the same design at Ithaca: the hazard of a machine's early reading 'is a property of single-verdict interfaces, not of machine reading as such', ranked alternatives are its mitigation, and Ithaca's gain comes from interface design, ranked hypotheses that the historian evaluates 'rather than accepting an answer' (#1443, §2.3); such systems 'work on authors who cannot be consulted' (#1443). The study sets itself beside Ithaca, which combined AI and epigraphy to date Greek inscriptions (PLOS One), and Haaretz's card opens 'From Ithaca to Judea Enoch is not the first artificial intelligence used to study ancient texts'; after it, Popović plans to apply the model to more scrolls and to Aramaic texts such as the Elephantine Papyri (Jerusalem Post), and Wikipedia records a five-year project he leads with the Israel Antiquities Authority, announced in June 2026, a distinct project. The study's limits stand with its findings: for 11Q5 it gives a date after 100 CE, against the reconstruction that the scrolls were hidden before summer 68 CE; its results are 'the first published results on date estimation for this collection', with validation to come, though it dates both halves of the Great Isaiah Scroll to one period; and its Herodian-type dates challenge the default typology, where 'More research is needed to solve this issue' (PLOS One). Reception divides, 'not all scholars are convinced' (BAS): Rollston finds the results 'not earth-shattering' and mostly what Frank Moore Cross had stated sixty years earlier, Ben-Dov finds points 'we would have otherwise missed' and asks whether the study is 'reliable enough to substantiate a re-shuffle of the entire chronological paradigm of Qumran', and Adler calls it 'a way to move forward' (BAS). The press gives the shift a size the study does not, which says 'often older': the Jerusalem Post, 'by 50 to 150 years earlier than previously believed', Popović, 'dates that are 50 years older or maybe even a century older', and a Reddit card, 'up to 100 years older'; video cards title it 'How AI Redated the Dead Sea Scrolls' and 'AI Just Decoded the Dead Sea Scrolls — What It Found Changes Everything', and a National Geographic UK post's title is cut at 'By combining time honoured excavation techniques'. At the name 'Enoch AI dating Dead Sea Scrolls' on Google's AI Overview, signed out, on 2026-10-31, a new address whose record was built the day before and which no card cites, the composition holds the study's figures, the 24 samples, the method, the roughly thirty-year error and 79% of 135, and keeps copies apart from their authors, 'the distinction the field turns on' (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31). The registry records its departures, 'a significant portion … 50 to 150 years older' for the study's 'often older', the radiocarbon date of 4Q114 credited to the model, figures for 4Q109 not in the saved sources, the study's own limit unsaid while doubt goes to Reddit and Popović's caution to Haaretz, and the study's frame surviving only as what 'Supporters view'; its reader noted the first two departures without charging them and found the funder and the commitments absent, and its analysis is that the study is 'composed nearly at its own grain', its 'figures grow where the press rounded them, and its doubts are sourced to a forum' (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31). The name is shared: the study says the model is 'named after the ancient Jewish science hero', and Wikipedia's disambiguation page gives the bare name as a biblical figure, the subject of the Book of Enoch, and lists no model (Wikipedia, Enoch (disambiguation)).

E_F.definition: Enoch, the AI-based date-prediction model of the Dead Sea Scrolls presented in 'Dating ancient manuscripts using radiocarbon and AI-based writing style analysis' (Popović, Dhali, Schomaker, van der Plicht, Lund Rasmussen, La Nasa et al., PLOS One 20(6): e0323185, 4 June 2025; Groningen and partners; ERC grant 640497, HandsandBible): Bayesian ridge regression on angular and allographic writing-style features of the ink trace, trained on 24 of 27 valid radiocarbon dates from 30 manuscripts, with errors of 27.9 to 30.7 years, applied to 135 undated scrolls (79% judged realistic by palaeographers among the authors); its finding, dates often older than the palaeographic estimates and a new chronology, with 4Q114 (by radiocarbon) and 4Q109 (by the model) the first known biblical fragments from the time of their presumed authors; its stated limits (radiocarbon superior, a first step, more research needed); received as unremarkable, promising or unproven (BAS), sized by the press at 50 to 150 years (JPost), and without a Wikipedia article (B1, B6, B2, B4, B10, B12, B13).
